**The states of the bound knower, and the way to the fourth** The knower, at bottom, is nothing other than the free conscious agent — his agency, his awareness, and his consciousness-self are primary. But the bound knower does not live in that freedom. He lives in a round of states — waking, dream, and deep sleep — which are the very texture of his bondage. To understand these states, and which of them lead him to his true nature, is the concern of this closing part of the vimarśa. At the lowest extreme is the state of the void. In the emptiness — where the intellect and the rest are absent — the "I-ness" and the "agent-ness" are only words. This is the dissolved knower, the pralayākala, absorbed in the void, with only the barest trace of an "I." His is a sleep without even a dream. Above that, the vital breath (prāṇa) stirs: it is the inner operation that stimulates the senses, the life that links the self to the organs. And with the breath come the three great states. Deep sleep (suṣupta) is like dissolution — a resting in the mere void or in the breath, where consciousness is put to sleep by māyā and not awakened even by the limited agency (kalā) or the limited knowledge (vidyā). It has two grades: with the known (the vidyākalā, still touched by the māyā-stain) and without the known (the pralayākala, free of the stain). Its many forms — sleep from fatigue, fainting from shock, intoxication and madness from wine, and even samādhi, the sleep of the yogin won by effort — are all species of this one deep-sleep state. The dream (svapna) is different. In the dream the senses are fixed and still, yet one sees the beloved and reaches out to touch her. Here only the mind is active, drawing on the prior creation, and making a clear, vivid world of its own — a momentary creation of the Lord within the dreamer. But in its sense-object part the dream shares the common world; and the moment we wake, the dream's clarity is refuted. So the dream is the mind's own making, a clear-appearance that the waking refutes. The waking state (jāgrat) is the common creation — the firm, external world shared by all the knowers. The waking knower is one who has shaken off the delusion-causing sleep. And yet, even here, the dream- form persists within the waking: the five states interpenetrate, each containing traces of the others. It is the difference of the known, Abhinavagupta notes, that spins out these many states of the one knower-ness. Now the crucial point. These three states — waking, dream, deep sleep — are to be *abandoned* by the seeker of liberation. For they are bound up with the vital breaths, with the primary-ness of the prāṇa in the agent, and with the rise and fall of pleasure and pain. The seeker, seeing this, regards the whole threefold round as the sphere to be left behind. The breath and the out-breath (prāṇa and apāna) run through waking and sleep; the udāna goes upward through the middle; but beyond them all is the fourth — the turya — the state that goes beyond the three, of the fire-form, the pure consciousness that is the goal. It is into this fourth that the recognition leads the bound knower, out of the round of the three, into the freedom that was always his own. With this, the dvitīyo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra — the analysis of the knowers, the stains, and the states — comes to its close. The bound soul has been fully mapped: its stains, its grades, its states, and its breaths. And the way out has been shown: through the recognition, from the three abandoned states to the fourth, the fire-form, the free consciousness-self. ---
